justification: Original value is genuinely high against the pages that rank for 'stack vs queue' / 'circular queue' / 'balanced parentheses stack'. GeeksforGeeks's balanced-parentheses page uses a generic '[()()]{}' example and stops at 'stack empty => balanced'; this article opens with a config-parser bug scenario, its own sample strings, and a naive counts-based checker that plausibly passes when it should not, which no compared page does. GfG's circular-queue page states the wraparound formulas but never dramatizes the moment the tail passes the physical end of the array or shows Capacity refusing to move under fill/drain/refill; this article builds RingQueue<T> from scratch, traces one Enqueue call's arithmetic by hand, diagrams it, and then proves Queue<T> really is circular by watching its own Capacity property. The List<T>-as-queue quadratic-cost measurement, the two-index empty/full ambiguity exercise, the RingQueue-to-RingDeque extension exercise, and the pushes==pops amortized argument (verified by an actual counting program, not asserted) are all original constructions with no equivalent in the compared pages. Five distinctive sentences of the writer's own prose, searched, returned no close matches elsewhere. No filler intro or outro: the first sentence states a concrete bug; the article ends inside a worked exercise solution rather than a generic 'Conclusion' or 'Key takeaways', which varies the pillar's ending pattern (arrays-and-dynamic-arrays ends with a 'Picking between...' decision table instead). No keyword stuffing, no ad code or ad placeholders. Toolchain statement ('The programs on this page compile and run with .NET 10 (runtime 10.0.12) on Windows 11, x64') sits in the second paragraph, directly beside the first real code block, not in the opening sentence -- matches the sibling article's placement and the pilot-round rule. Structure is not templated against arrays-and-dynamic-arrays.md: headings, section order and phrasing are unrelated (memory-layout/cache framing there vs LIFO/FIFO-contract framing here), and no boilerplate 'Introduction'/'Conclusion' headings appear in either. Exercises are four genuinely different forms (find-the-bug on a broken ring buffer, extend-the-code into a deque, predict-the-output on Count/Capacity, adapt-the-code from next-greater-value to next-greater-distance), none give away their output before the solution is expanded, and they sit mid-article rather than bunched in a trailing 'Exercises' section. The self-reported explicit-interface `System.Collections.IEnumerator IEnumerable.GetEnumerator()` fix is invisible in prose -- it never gets a sentence of its own, appears identically and silently in both RingQueue<T> and RingDeque<T>, and does not read as awkward or distracting. The monotonic-stack section's tie to /complexity/amortized-analysis/ ('the same amortized argument that makes List<T>.Add O(1)... charge the cost somewhere it cannot be exceeded in total') is a real conceptual link (charging/banker's-style argument in both places), not a bolted-on mention, and that route exists in the build. `run-code.mjs` PASS, blocks=25 executed=12, exactly as claimed. `npm run build` is green (32 pages; the article itself is excluded as draft:true, as expected) and the /complexity/amortized-analysis/ target it cross-links to is a live route. Microsoft Learn and dotnet/runtime claims were independently re-fetched and check out exactly: 'Stack<T> is implemented as an array', 'this class implements a generic queue as a circular array', List<T>.RemoveAt's 'O(n) operation, where n is (Count - index)', Queue.cs's MoveNext body verbatim, and the doubling/minimum-growth-of-4 policy for both Stack<T> and Queue<T>. Against that strength sits one serious problem: a fabricated quotation attributed to a real, listed, accessed source (see issue 1), which is exactly the class of thing the binding rules and the pilot lessons single out, and two more front-matter sources that are never cited in the body at all. The fabrication caps this well below the pass bar regardless of how strong the rest of the page is; the article is not at the bar this round.

issues.location: 'A next-greater-element with a monotonic stack', paragraph 1: '"maintain[ing] a deque in a state, where they are monotonically increasing (or decreasing)"'; front matter source 'Stack / queue modifications (minimum stack, monotonic deque)' -> https://cp-algorithms.com/data_structures/stack_queue_modification.html
issues.problem: This is presented as a direct quotation (quotation marks, with a bracketed word-form edit that signals 'copied verbatim, tense adjusted') attributed by name to cp-algorithms. I fetched the cited page twice, once for its raw section-by-section content. The word 'monotonic' (or any form of it) does not appear anywhere on that page, and no sentence resembles the quoted one. What the page actually says is: 'we will keep the queue in nondecreasing order (i.e. the smallest value will be stored in the head)' and 'we will remove all trailing elements of the queue that are larger than the new element, and afterwards add the new element to the queue' -- a real idea, but not the words quoted, and the page's real title is 'Minimum stack / Minimum queue', not the 'monotonic deque' framing given it in front matter. This is a fabricated quotation attached to a real source: exactly what the binding rule 'Never fabricate anything... no invented... quotes' and the pilot lesson 'make sure that page supports that clause' exist to catch. It would be trivially caught by anyone who followed the link, including an AdSense reviewer.
issues.fixLooksLike: Drop the quotation marks and the bracketed edit. Paraphrase honestly from what the page says, e.g.: 'cp-algorithms describes the same idea for a minimum-tracking queue: keep it in nondecreasing order by removing every trailing element larger than the new one before adding it (Method 1).' Fix the front-matter source title to match the page's actual title ('Minimum stack / Minimum queue') or drop the parenthetical 'monotonic deque' gloss, since the source itself never uses that term.
